revisions.explanation:
Sample composition:
The Importance of Reading Books

Books open doors to knowledge, imagination and understanding. A reader can learn about distant places, meet characters from different backgrounds and explore ideas that may not appear in a classroom lesson. Reading is therefore both useful and enjoyable.

Different books serve different purposes. Textbooks explain school subjects, while stories help us imagine how other people feel. Biographies introduce the lives and efforts of individuals, and science books encourage us to ask questions about the world. A newspaper or a reference book can also help us find information, although we should check important claims against reliable sources.

Regular reading develops vocabulary and improves writing. It teaches us to concentrate and gives us time away from the constant noise of screens. A library makes this habit affordable because many readers can share the same books. Students should choose age-appropriate books, look after them and return borrowed copies on time.

A reading group can introduce a student to unfamiliar authors and different ways of telling a story. Members should explain their opinions with examples instead of simply announcing that a book is good.

I try to read for a short period each day. When a word is unfamiliar, I note it down and look up its meaning. Later I discuss an interesting passage with a friend. Reading does not mean accepting every idea without thought; it means considering ideas carefully and asking questions. In this way books become companions as well as teachers. A steady reading habit can enrich our lives for many years.

Tree Plantation

Trees are essential to a healthy environment. They provide shade, shelter for wildlife and useful products such as fruit and timber. Their roots help hold soil in place, while their leaves contribute to the natural processes that support life. Planting and protecting trees is therefore an important responsibility.

In many places trees are cut down to make room for roads, buildings or farms. Some development is necessary, but careless removal can leave land exposed to erosion and reduce habitats for birds and other animals. In hot weather, a tree-lined playground or street can also offer welcome shade. Planting suitable trees can help restore some of these benefits.

A successful plantation requires more than putting a sapling in the ground. We should choose species suited to the local environment and plant them in places where their roots and branches have enough space. A teacher, gardener or local expert can help select an appropriate site. Young trees need water, protection and regular attention, especially during dry weather.

Choosing a suitable species matters as much as arranging a large planting ceremony in a public place. Roots need enough space, and young plants require protection from animals and careless movement.

Schools can organise supervised planting days and prepare a watering schedule. Communities can also protect existing trees and replace those lost to storms or disease. Everyone can take part by caring for a plant or learning why local species matter. If we combine careful planting with long-term care, the trees we nurture today can benefit future generations.

A Journey by Train

A journey by train can be both comfortable and memorable. Last winter I travelled with my family to visit relatives in another town. It was my first long train journey, and I was excited from the moment we reached the station.

The platform was busy with passengers carrying bags and looking for their coaches. We checked our tickets and waited safely behind the platform edge. When the train arrived, we found our seats and placed our luggage where it would not block the aisle. Soon the train began to move, and the station slowly disappeared from view.

Through the window I saw fields, ponds and small houses. At some stations people got on while others waved goodbye to their families. My mother shared snacks, and my father pointed out a river as we crossed a bridge. I enjoyed watching the changing landscape and talking with my younger brother. We also made sure not to throw any waste out of the window.

At a station, clear signs and helpful staff make the journey easier for passengers who are unfamiliar with the route. Travellers should keep their tickets safely and allow others to leave before boarding.

The journey took several hours, but I did not feel bored. When we reached our destination, our relatives were waiting to welcome us. The trip taught me that a journey is not merely a way to reach a place; it can also be a chance to observe people, enjoy nature and spend time with family.

The Duties of a Student

Student life is a time for learning, building good habits and discovering interests. A student's main duty is to study sincerely, but education includes much more than memorising lessons for examinations. It also involves responsibility towards family, school and the wider community.

A responsible student attends classes regularly, listens carefully and asks questions when a lesson is unclear. Preparing a realistic timetable helps balance schoolwork, rest and recreation. Students should complete their own work honestly instead of using unfair means. A mistake is an opportunity to learn, and teachers can help when a topic is difficult.

Good behaviour matters as well. We should respect teachers, parents and classmates, and we should never make fun of someone who learns differently. Keeping the classroom clean and taking care of shared books show respect for school property. During group work, students can listen to different opinions and share tasks fairly.

A student also has duties when working with others on a project rather than studying alone. Sharing tasks fairly allows quieter classmates to participate and develop confidence in their own abilities. Asking a question politely is more useful than pretending to understand a difficult lesson.

Students also need exercise, adequate sleep and time for creative activities. Joining a club or taking part in a supervised community project can develop cooperation and confidence. Above all, learning should help us become thoughtful and kind citizens. By doing our duties regularly, we prepare ourselves not only for examinations but also for the responsibilities of adult life.

Physical Exercise

Physical exercise is an important part of a healthy life. It keeps the body active and can help us feel refreshed. Walking, cycling, swimming and playing games are examples of exercise, and different people may enjoy different activities.

Regular movement helps develop strength and fitness. Team games can also teach cooperation, patience and respect for rules. Exercise gives students a break from long hours of sitting and studying. It can be more enjoyable when friends or family members participate together. However, exercise alone is not enough: healthy food, safe drinking water and sufficient sleep are important too.

We should choose activities that suit our age and health. Beginners can start gently and gradually increase their activity. It is wise to warm up, use appropriate equipment and drink water when needed. Playing in a safe place and following a coach's instructions can reduce the risk of injury. Anyone with an illness or medical concern should ask a qualified health professional for advice.

Exercise should be suited to a person's age, abilities and health rather than copied blindly from others. A safe space, comfortable clothing and enough drinking water can make regular activity more enjoyable.

I enjoy walking and playing badminton with my friends. These activities make me feel energetic and help me return to my studies with a clear mind. The best routine is one that is safe and enjoyable enough to follow regularly. By making room for movement in our daily lives, we can support our physical and mental well-being.

A Book Fair

A book fair brings readers, writers and publishers together. It offers a pleasant opportunity to discover books, share ideas and celebrate the habit of reading. I visited a book fair with my classmates and a teacher last year, and the experience remains fresh in my mind.

The fair was held in a large open area with rows of colourful stalls. Publishers displayed storybooks, poems, children's magazines and books on science and history. Visitors moved from stall to stall, examining covers and discussing their favourite authors. Some stalls had small spaces where writers spoke to readers about their work.

I was especially interested in a collection of short stories. Before buying it, I read the description and compared its price with another edition. My friend chose a book about birds, while our teacher recommended a biography for the school library. We also attended a reading session where a writer answered questions from children.

A fair should also be welcoming to visitors who cannot afford to buy many expensive books. Reading corners, accessible paths and affordable editions can help more people take part in the event.

A book fair is more than a place to buy things. It encourages people to explore new ideas and helps young readers develop curiosity. Those who cannot buy many books can still discover titles to look for in a library. We returned home tired but happy, carrying books and many ideas to discuss. I hope to visit another fair soon.

The Importance of Clean Water

Clean water is essential for life. People need safe water for drinking, cooking and personal hygiene, and farmers need it to grow crops. Animals and plants also depend on water, so protecting water sources benefits the whole environment.

Water can become polluted when rubbish, sewage or harmful chemicals enter rivers, ponds and other sources. Drinking contaminated water can cause illness. For this reason families should use a safe supply and follow local health guidance on treating water when necessary. Storing drinking water in clean, covered containers also helps protect it from contamination.

Everyone can help reduce waste and pollution. We can turn off taps after use, report leaking pipes and avoid throwing plastic or other rubbish into water. Communities and local authorities have important roles in managing waste, protecting sources and maintaining safe water systems. Schools can teach students how water reaches their homes and why cleanliness matters.

Saving clean water is another responsibility because treatment and distribution require money, energy and careful maintenance. A leaking tap should be reported promptly instead of being ignored as a small problem. Storing water in a covered, clean container can help protect it from contamination at home.

During a flood or other emergency, a normally safe source may become contaminated. In such circumstances we should listen to reliable local advice rather than assume the water is safe. Clean water should be available to everyone, not treated as a luxury. By using it carefully and working together to protect it, we support health, farming and the natural world.

The garden is useful in several ways. Students can observe leaves, flowers and insects rather than learning about them only from pictures. Working in a group teaches us patience and cooperation. The flowers make the school cheerful, while the vegetables show how food can be grown. We avoid damaging nests or insects and ask an adult before using any gardening tools.

Keeping a garden notebook helps students compare what happens in different parts of the growing area. A garden committee should share responsibilities so that maintenance does not depend on one enthusiastic student.

A garden needs regular care, including during holidays. For this reason we make a schedule and ask school staff to supervise the work. I enjoy watching a seedling grow over several weeks. Our garden reminds us that a small effort, repeated patiently, can create something beautiful and useful.

The Value of Time

Time is one of the most valuable resources in life. Once a moment has passed, we cannot bring it back. Learning to use time wisely helps students complete their duties while still leaving room for rest, friendship and enjoyment.

A timetable is a useful guide, but it should be realistic. We can set aside time for school lessons, homework, exercise and sleep. Difficult tasks may be divided into smaller steps so that they do not feel overwhelming. Starting revision early can reduce pressure before an examination. When plans change, we can adjust them instead of giving up altogether.

Using time well does not mean working without a break. Rest and recreation are necessary for health and concentration. The problem arises when an activity continues so long that important duties are repeatedly neglected. For example, setting a reasonable limit on screen use can leave more time for reading or playing outdoors.

Using time wisely does not mean filling every minute with study and refusing all recreation or rest. A realistic timetable includes meals, sleep, exercise and time spent listening to family members and friends. Unexpected difficulties may require a plan to change, so flexibility is as important as punctuality.

Punctuality also shows respect for other people's time. Arriving on time for school and keeping promises help build trust. At the same time, we should be understanding when someone faces circumstances beyond their control. By planning carefully and choosing our priorities, we can make each day more balanced and meaningful.

A Rainy Day

A rainy day brings a special change to the familiar landscape. Dark clouds gather, the air becomes cooler and the sound of falling rain fills the surroundings. Some people enjoy the change, while others face difficulties travelling or working outdoors.

One morning last monsoon, rain began just as I was preparing for school. I carried an umbrella and walked carefully along the wet road with my neighbour. Trees looked freshly washed, and small drops hung from their leaves. At school many students arrived with wet shoes, but our teachers made sure we entered the classrooms safely.

Rain is valuable for farming and for replenishing water in ponds and rivers. Yet heavy rainfall can also cause waterlogging and make roads slippery. People who work outside may lose income when they cannot work. We should therefore appreciate the rain while remembering those who need help during difficult weather.

Rain also affects people differently, depending on their homes, occupations and the condition of nearby roads. While some enjoy the cool weather, others struggle to travel or keep their workplaces dry. We should avoid walking through unknown floodwater and should listen to responsible adults about safer routes.

After school I stayed indoors, read a story and listened to the rain on the roof. In the evening the clouds cleared and the garden looked bright again. That day reminded me of both the beauty and the responsibilities that come with the rainy season. Keeping drains clear and following local safety advice can help our communities cope better when rain is heavy.

Buyers compare prices and choose what they need. The calls of vendors and the conversations of customers make the place lively.

The market also gives neighbours a chance to exchange news and meet people they do not see every day. Prices may change with the season, so families must plan their spending. Treating sellers and buyers fairly makes this busy gathering more useful to everyone.

The market helps farmers sell their produce without travelling to a distant town. It also gives small traders an opportunity to earn a living. However, waste and muddy paths can cause inconvenience. Proper bins, clean water and regular cleaning would make the market safer and more pleasant. A well-managed village market serves both the local economy and the community.

A library becomes more useful when its collection reflects the different interests and reading levels of students. A suggestion box can help the librarian understand which books readers would like to borrow. Clear labels and a simple borrowing record make it easier for everyone to find and return materials.

We must follow some simple rules. We should speak softly, handle books carefully and return them on time. Writing on pages or tearing them prevents others from enjoying the same books. My Favourite Hobby

My favourite hobby is gardening. It gives me pleasure and teaches me to be patient. I do not need a large field; a few pots on a balcony or a small patch of soil can be enough to begin.

I grow flowers and some vegetables with help from my family. First, I loosen the soil and choose healthy seeds or seedlings. I water the plants when they need it and remove weeds carefully. Sometimes insects damage the leaves, so I ask an experienced gardener for safe advice rather than using chemicals carelessly.

I keep a small notebook to record what I plant and how it grows. This helps me remember which pots receive enough sunlight. When I share extra seedlings with a neighbour, my hobby becomes a way to build friendship as well as care for nature.

A hobby should remain enjoyable rather than become another competition in which every result must be perfect. I can set a small personal goal and notice improvements without comparing myself constantly with others. Sharing my interests with friends sometimes introduces me to useful ideas and different methods of working.

The most exciting moment comes when a seedling produces its first flower or fruit. Not every plant survives, but a failure helps me learn about sunlight, water and soil. Gardening also makes our surroundings greener. It gives me a useful break from study and reminds me that living things need steady care. I hope to continue this hobby as I grow older.

A Journey by Boat

Last autumn I went on a boat journey with my family. We visited relatives who live across a river. The sky was clear, and the water shone in the morning sunlight.

Before boarding, we checked that the boat was not overcrowded and followed the boatman's instructions. I sat beside my mother and watched the banks move slowly past us. Fishermen were working in small boats, and children waved from near their homes. Green fields and patches of trees stretched beyond the water.

At one point a larger vessel passed at a distance, and our boat rocked gently in its wake. I held the side of my seat and listened to the boatman. He knew the route well, and his calm manner made the passengers feel comfortable.

Before boarding, passengers should check that the boat is not overcrowded and follow the crew's safety instructions. A properly fitted life jacket is more useful than confidence in one's ability to swim. Weather conditions can change, so postponing a trip may be wiser than taking an unnecessary risk.

The boatman told us how the river changes with the seasons. We carried our own drinking water and kept our bags away from the edge. After a peaceful journey, we reached the other bank, where our relatives welcomed us. I enjoyed the scenery and learned that a river is both a beautiful part of nature and an important route for local people. The memory of the trip still makes me happy.

A Winter Morning

A winter morning has a special beauty in Bangladesh. The air is cool, and fog often covers fields, roads and trees. People may wake to find drops of dew on grass and spiderwebs.

In villages, farmers begin their work despite the cold. Some people gather around a small fire to warm themselves. As the sun rises, the fog slowly disappears and the surroundings become clearer. Families may enjoy warm pitha and date juice where these are available and safely prepared.

On the way to school, I enjoy watching sunlight appear through the mist. People walk briskly in sweaters and shawls, and shops gradually open for the day. By noon, the warmth of the sun makes the morning cold seem like a distant memory.

A winter morning can also remind us that comfort is not equally available to every family. People who work outdoors may need warm clothing long before others leave their beds. Donating clean, usable clothes through a reliable local group is one practical way of helping. Winter is pleasant for many people, but it can be difficult for those who lack warm clothes or shelter. We can share clean blankets and clothing through trustworthy local groups. We should also take care around fires and help younger children stay warm. A winter morning is memorable not only for its natural beauty but also for the kindness it can inspire among neighbours.

I must learn about the training, responsibilities and ethical choices involved in my chosen work. I hope one day to serve in a community where medical services are limited. I would treat patients with respect and encourage them to seek reliable health advice. My goal may be difficult, but it motivates me to use my time well. Whatever profession I finally choose, I want my work to benefit others.

To improve English, we should practise reading, writing, listening and speaking regularly. Simple stories, conversations and class activities can make practice enjoyable.

Learning English should help us exchange ideas without making us feel ashamed of our own mother tongue. Progress is usually gradual, but regular practice makes an unfamiliar language increasingly useful.

Mistakes are a natural part of learning. Instead of being afraid, students should ask for help and try again. Keeping a vocabulary notebook and using new words in sentences can be useful. With patience and regular practice, we can become more confident. English is a practical skill that can open opportunities while allowing us to share our own culture with others.

The building impressed me with its thick walls, rows of pillars and many domes. A guide explained that it was associated with Khan Jahan Ali and the medieval settlement of Khalifatabad. I listened carefully and tried to imagine the people who had lived and worked in the area centuries ago.

The Importance of Road Safety

Road safety is a shared responsibility. Pedestrians, drivers, passengers and authorities all have roles in reducing accidents. Careful behaviour and safe road design can protect lives.

Pedestrians should use footpaths and marked crossings where available. Before crossing, they should look carefully in both directions and avoid being distracted by a phone. Children may need help from an adult on busy roads. Passengers should wait in a safe place and avoid boarding a moving vehicle.

Drivers should obey speed limits, follow traffic signals and never drive while distracted or impaired. Authorities can improve safety by maintaining roads, providing crossings and enforcing traffic rules fairly. Schools can teach students how to identify hazards and practise safe travel.

At school, a supervised discussion can help students identify dangerous places near the gate. They can share their observations with teachers, who may raise concerns with the appropriate authorities. Safe routes need attention from the whole community, not just individual travellers.

Road safety improves when people recognise that a small careless action can affect many others around them. Pedestrians should use suitable crossings where available and remain attentive instead of looking only at a phone. Drivers and passengers also have responsibilities, including using appropriate restraints and following traffic rules.

No single action can prevent every accident, and people do not always have access to safe infrastructure. Nevertheless, attention, planning and cooperation can make journeys safer for everyone. We should treat road safety as a daily duty rather than an occasional concern.

A School Magazine

A school magazine is a collection of writing and artwork produced by students and teachers. It may include poems, stories, essays, drawings and reports about school activities. The magazine gives young writers a chance to share their ideas.

To prepare an issue, an editorial team invites contributions and selects suitable work. Teachers can help students correct language and check facts without removing their individual voices. Contributors should submit their own work or acknowledge any material they use with permission. The team then organises the pages and checks the final copy before publication.

Students can learn useful skills by interviewing people, planning deadlines and revising drafts. They also learn to accept suggestions without taking criticism personally. When the finished issue appears, contributors can take pride in the teamwork that made it possible.

Producing a school magazine also teaches students that publication brings responsibilities towards writers, readers and people mentioned in articles. The editorial team should check facts, correct spelling and obtain permission for material that belongs to others. Different students can contribute drawings, reports, poems or practical help according to their interests. Sharing these tasks makes the magazine a genuine school project rather than the work of a small, familiar group.

A magazine encourages creativity, cooperation and careful reading. A student who is shy in class may find confidence through a poem or illustration. A printed or digital edition can also preserve memories of the school year. If everyone has a fair opportunity to contribute, the magazine becomes a lively record of the whole school community.

Sample composition:
The Uses and Abuses of the Internet

The internet connects people to information and services across the world. Students can use it to attend lessons, consult reference materials and communicate with teachers. It also helps people find news, conduct business and stay in touch with relatives.

However, not everything online is reliable. False information can spread quickly, so important claims should be checked against trustworthy sources. Spending too much time on games or social media can also interfere with sleep and study. Online strangers may try to trick people into sharing personal information.

A website can look convincing even when its information is inaccurate. Checking the author, date and evidence, and comparing claims with other reliable sources, helps readers make better judgments. We should be especially cautious before sharing alarming messages or financial information.

Useful internet habits include taking regular breaks and deciding why we are opening a site before becoming distracted. Personal photographs, passwords and private messages should be handled carefully, even when sharing seems convenient. A troubling online experience should be discussed with a trusted adult rather than hidden out of embarrassment. With guidance and self-control, young people can benefit from digital resources while recognising their limits and risks.

We should use strong passwords, keep them private and ask a trusted adult for help when something seems suspicious. It is wise to think before posting and to treat others respectfully. A balanced schedule leaves time for study, exercise and family. The internet is a useful tool when we use it carefully, critically and with respect for our own safety and that of others.
